title: Descriptive statistics on right-skewed healthcare claims
concept: Analysts report numbers; data scientists ask how those numbers are distributed and how sure we can be about them. Key ideas: mean vs. median (skew pulls the mean toward the tail), standard deviation, percentiles and IQR (Q3 − Q1), outliers via the 1.5×IQR rule, and the log1p transform to tame right skew. Healthcare claim amounts are heavily right-skewed, so the median and log transforms matter a lot.
steps: Create a GitHub repo ds-genai-90-days with folders day01/, data/ and a README.md.
In day01/descriptive_stats.ipynb, simulate 5,000 claims with np.random.lognormal(mean=6, sigma=1, size=5000), plus member_id and plan_type (HMO/PPO).
Compute mean, median, std, skew and percentiles overall and by plan type with groupby().describe().
Plot histograms of raw vs. np.log1p amounts.
Write 3 stakeholder-style insights in a markdown cell.
Stretch: reproduce the stats in Snowflake with MEDIAN and PERCENTILE_CONT.

snippets.title: 1. Environment
snippets.code:
conda create -n ds90 python=3.11 pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn scipy jupyter -y
conda activate ds90

snippets.title: 2. Simulate claims & describe
snippets.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 5000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "member_id": rng.integers(1000, 2000, n),
    "plan_type": rng.choice(["HMO", "PPO"], n),
    "amount": np.random.lognormal(mean=6, sigma=1, size=n),
})
print(df["amount"].agg(["mean", "median", "std", "skew"]))
print(df.groupby("plan_type")["amount"].describe())

snippets.title: 3. IQR outliers & log1p histograms
snippets.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

q1, q3 = df["amount"].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
cutoff = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
df["is_outlier"] = df["amount"] > cutoff
print(f"IQR={iqr:.0f}, cutoff={cutoff:.0f}, outliers={df.is_outlier.sum()}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
ax[0].hist(df["amount"], bins=60); ax[0].set_title("Raw amounts")
ax[1].hist(np.log1p(df["amount"]), bins=60); ax[1].set_title("log1p(amount)")
plt.show()

snippets.title: Stretch: Snowflake SQL
snippets.code:
SELECT plan_type,
       AVG(amount) AS mean_amt,
       MEDIAN(amount) AS median_amt,
       STDDEV(amount) AS std_amt,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS q1,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS q3
FROM claims
GROUP BY plan_type;

podcast: Welcome to Day One of the Data Science Coach podcast, where you go from data analyst to data scientist with Gen AI skills, one day at a time. Today's topic is descriptive statistics, and why the mean can lie to you.

Picture a table of healthcare claims. Most claims are small, a few hundred dollars for an office visit or a lab test. But every so often there's a huge one, a surgery or a hospital stay that costs tens of thousands. That pattern is called right skew.

The mean gets pulled toward that long tail. In our practice data, the mean claim is about six hundred fifty dollars, but the median is only about four hundred. With skewed data, the median tells the honest story.

Standard deviation is inflated by skew too. A sturdier measure of spread is the interquartile range: the seventy-fifth percentile minus the twenty-fifth. Here it's about five hundred fifty-six dollars.

The IQR gives a classic outlier rule: anything more than one and a half IQRs above the third quartile. Our cutoff is around sixteen hundred dollars, flagging about four hundred claims. In healthcare, those outliers are often the high-cost members a care management team wants to find.
Taking the log, with numpy's log one p, squeezes the long tail so the distribution looks closer to a bell curve, which many machine learning models prefer.
The mindset shift: an analyst reports the average. A data scientist first checks the distribution, then picks the right summary.
Tomorrow we move from describing data to making decisions with it: probability distributions and the foundations of hypothesis testing. See you then.
